node.label: Karen Dubinsky
node.date_label: Improper Advances (1993) · “Beyond Purity,” with Lynne Marks (1996) · The Second Greatest Disappointment (1999) · Babies Without Borders (2010) · Within and Without the Nation, co-edited (2015)
node.description: In Improper Advances (1993), Karen Dubinsky argued that sexual violence in Ontario must be understood through unequal power and through women’s distinction between desired and coerced sex. Reading criminal case files, she treated women as sexual agents who sought pleasure and challenged coercion despite hostile courts and communities. With Lynne Marks, “Beyond Purity” (1996) defended the compatibility of women’s and gender history and the value of studying masculinity. Joan Sangster’s reply disputed their account of her position and insisted that gender history’s merits did not establish its automatic superiority. The Second Greatest Disappointment (1999) extended Dubinsky’s work on sexuality to honeymooning and tourism at Niagara Falls. Babies Without Borders (2010) questioned accounts of adoption organized entirely around rescue or kidnap. Reviewing it in 2011, Ferzana Chaze praised that challenge but found its treatment of Indigenous adoption less persuasive because the socioeconomic pressures it described could themselves be seen as results of the historical oppression and marginalisation of Aboriginal communities in Canada. Dubinsky also coedited Within and Without the Nation (2015), with Adele Perry and Henry Yu.
node.representative_figures_and_works: With Franca Iacovetta, “Murder, Womanly Virtue, and Motherhood” (1991); Improper Advances: Rape and Heterosexual Conflict in Ontario, 1880–1929 (1993); with Lynne Marks, “Beyond Purity: A Response to Sangster” (1996); The Second Greatest Disappointment: Honeymooning and Tourism at Niagara Falls (1999); Babies Without Borders: Adoption and Migration Across the Americas (2010); with Adele Perry and Henry Yu, eds., Within and Without the Nation: Canadian History as Transnational History (2015).
node.scope_note: “Beyond Purity” (1996) and Sangster’s reply (1996) read in full in archived journal PDFs; selected methodological and attribution passages from the publisher’s 2010 chapter sample read; Chaze’s 2011 review read in full. Improper Advances known here through its publisher description; the 1999 book, 2010 monograph and 2015 collection are not read in full. Coauthor/editor credits and selected years checked against the author CV and publisher metadata. Earlier works invoked by the 1996 respondents are not independently re-read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Dubinsky and Franca Iacovetta coauthored “Murder, Womanly Virtue, and Motherhood: The Case of Angelina Napolitano” (1991).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Dubinsky’s own CV, printed p. 16, explicitly credits Iacovetta and gives Canadian Historical Review, December 1991, pp. 505–531; p. 3 records their joint article prize. Bibliographic collaboration only: the article body was not read and no joint argument or influence is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Dubinsky, Adele Perry and Henry Yu coedited Within and Without the Nation: Canadian History as Transnational History (2015).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher/distributor page, title and Edited by line, publication date November 2015; author CV printed p. 11 corroborates joint credit. This is a co-editing relationship, not a claim that one editor influenced another. Collection and introduction unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity: A Response to Sangster” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks reject Sangster’s opposition between women’s and gender history and argue that gender analysis can strengthen feminist history without replacing women’s history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh complete journal-archive PDF read, pp. 205–220; especially pp. 205–211 and 218–220. On p. 207 they say there is “no need to choose” between the approaches. Their qualification on pp. 218–219 acknowledges the risks of detached category analysis. Joint intervention, not Dubinsky alone; Sangster’s original 1995 essay not independently read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Reconsidering Dichotomies” (1996), Sangster criticizes Dubinsky and Lynne Marks for attributing to her a rejection of gender history and for reproducing oppositions in their response, while conceding that her own account had blurred separate theoretical questions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh complete archived journal PDF read, pp. 239–248. P. 242 explicitly identifies the Dubinsky–Marks opening metaphor; pp. 243–244 reject the positions assigned to her and concede that the original essay “blurred two issues”; p. 248 rejects their description of her position as narrow. This incoming reply is distinct from the outgoing response and is not a criticism of every Dubinsky book.
proposed_edges.map_label: Sangster replies to Dubinsky and Marks

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks use Joy Parr’s The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) and “Gender History and Historical Practice” (1995) to support a contextual account of identity that gives no single category automatic priority.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; p. 211 and n. 11 explicitly attribute the point to Parr, rejecting imposition of “one category”; p. 209 n. 6 also cites the 1990 book. This is documented conceptual use in the joint essay, not supervision or a career-wide lineage. Parr’s two originals not independently re-read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks use Linda Gordon’s Pitied But Not Entitled (1994) to show how gender analysis can connect women’s lives to the social policies and competing visions of the welfare state.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; pp. 206–207 and n. 2 identify Gordon’s book and discuss social insurance and social work as differing gendered visions. The term “analytic” on p. 207 marks the methodological use. Gordon’s book remains unread here; this is the respondents’ uptake, not an independent judgment of her full argument.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses Gordon on gender and welfare

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks draw on John Tosh’s work on masculinity to argue that treating men as an unmarked norm hides the operation of gendered power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; p. 214 n. 15 credits Michael Roper and Tosh’s coauthored introduction to Manful Assertions (1991); p. 217 and n. 20 explicitly use Tosh’s “What Should Historians Do with Masculinity?” (1994), p. 180, to explain the invisibility of masculinity. Short phrase: “relational concept” (p. 214). Credit to Roper retained; neither original newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks praise Catherine Hall and Leonore Davidoff’s Family Fortunes (1987) for treating masculine power as socially made, but find it insufficiently attentive to consent and coercion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; p. 214 and n. 14 name both authors and the 1987 book, contrasting its historically constructed account with Rotundo’s before calling it “too quiet” on consent and coercion. Their further use of the book on p. 217 shows this is qualified criticism. Joint credit retained on both sides; Family Fortunes itself not newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks quote Anna Clark’s 1993 Journal of Women’s History comment for the problem of how to link postmodernist attention to language with historical questions of power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete response read; pp. 218–219 and n. 22 explicitly attribute the problem of linking linguistic analysis to “questions of power” to Anna Clark’s 1993 Journal of Women’s History comment. Her 1995 book is also cited in n. 3 but does not by itself support this edge. The comment remains unread independently. Endpoint is another candidate in this run.
proposed_edges.map_label: Cites Clark on language and power

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Haven from Racism? Canadians Imagine Interracial Adoption” (2010), Dubinsky invokes Veronica Strong-Boag’s warning against idealizing a uniform Indigenous family past.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, p. 24 and n. 52 on p. 32, explicitly attributes the caution “not to glamorize” to Strong-Boag’s Finding Families, Finding Ourselves (2006), p. 138. That book is unread here. Claim is limited to a scholarly caution; no family stories, narrator quotations or community knowledge are reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: Improper Advances (1993) contributes to Canadian women’s and gender history by analyzing sexual coercion and unequal power alongside women’s sexual agency in Ontario criminal case files.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description, paragraphs 1–4, and 1993 copyright read; complete book unread. The claim follows the publisher’s account, not a fresh reading of its case studies. This field already has a Dubinsky roster row, which is preserved.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks defend gender history as an analysis of power that includes masculinity and connects categories of meaning with lived experience.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete joint essay read, especially pp. 207–211 and 214–220. At p. 218 “gender is present” introduces their use of Ava Baron; the same page warns against an apolitical study of categories. This describes a methodological contribution rather than blanket adherence to poststructuralism.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Haven from Racism? Canadians Imagine Interracial Adoption” (2010), Dubinsky makes children’s symbolic power a problem for Canadian childhood history and questions explanations of adoption framed solely as rescue or kidnap.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, pp. 15–16, opening methodological statement; phrase “symbolic power” on p. 15. The entire book is unread, and the edge does not reproduce the chapter’s individual histories or generalize its limited archive into community-wide findings.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beyond Purity” (1996), Dubinsky and Lynne Marks use Anne McClintock’s Imperial Leather (1995) to argue that gender is integral to imperial power and that feminist historical inquiry can combine several theoretical approaches.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete joint response read, especially p. 206 and n. 1. They explicitly discuss Imperial Leather, quote its argument about gender and imperial power, and praise its combination of historical materialism, poststructuralism and psychoanalytic approaches as “non-sectarian”. This is specific uptake in the response; McClintock’s book remains unread independently and no personal mentorship is inferred.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses McClintock on gender and empire

proposed_edges.relationship: In her historiographical essay “The History of Us” (2000), Cynthia Comacchio discusses Karen Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) and The Second Greatest Disappointment (1999) as Foucault-informed studies of the spatial, class and gender dimensions of sexuality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s PDF discussion on pp. 191–195. Comacchio substantively uses both books to explain historical sexuality, rather than merely listing citations. This is uptake in a historiographical synthesis, not evidence that Dubinsky originated Comacchio’s research programme. The books themselves were not read for this task.

proposed_edges.relationship: Karen Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) contributed to the history of sexuality by examining heterosexual coercion and women’s agency through the interacting inequalities of gender, class and ethnicity, as Christina Simmons assessed in “A Proper Account of Improper Sex” (1994).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Simmons’s ten-page review in the journal’s PDF. She explicitly evaluates the book’s contribution to sexuality history while also criticizing its presentation and limited account of change over time. The endpoint includes sexuality history; this claim does not make the book a study of queer identities. The monograph itself was not read.
